item.title: Radiative effects of decreased North America and European aerosols weaken the AMOC via wind-driven freshwater advection
item.dc:creator: Xuyang Li, Fukai Liu, Yiyong Luo, Xiao-Tong Zheng
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Greenland, Arctic, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, coupled climate model, model intercomparison, CMIP, radiative forcing, ensemble
Abstract Growing observational and modeling evidence suggests that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has weakened since the 1980s, with reductions in North American and European (NAEU) aerosols identified as a potential contributing factor. Here we use fully coupled climate model experiments to demonstrate that the radiative forcing associated with decreased NAEU aerosols weakens the AMOC by enhancing freshwater transport from the Arctic and subtropical regions into the deep convection region. Reduced aerosol loading induces large-scale atmospheric circulation adjustments, including cyclonic wind stress anomalies over the Arctic Ocean and the subtropical North Atlantic. Over the Arctic Ocean, the cyclonic wind stress anomaly weakens the Beaufort Gyre, releasing freshwater that accumulates north of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Greenland. This freshwater is then exported through Baffin Bay into the Labrador Sea, suppressing deep convection there. Simultaneously, enhanced cyclonic wind stress over the subtropical North Atlantic weakens the North Atlantic Current (NAC), reducing the northward transport of saline water and promoting the freshwater accumulation within the subpolar gyre. This freshwater anomaly is then advected toward the Labrador Sea, further suppressing deep convection and weakening the AMOC. Together, our results identify a remotely driven pathway through which reductions in NAEU aerosols weaken the AMOC via wind-driven freshwater advection. The robustness of this mechanism is further supported by the multi-model ensemble mean from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) simulations, which exhibits consistent oceanic and atmospheric circulation responses.

item.title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
item.dc:creator: Xiyu Dong, Xu Zhang, Yuchen Sun, Gayatri Kathayat, Youwei Li, Sune Olander Rasmussen, … (+19)
item.description:
Science — matched: Greenland, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, ocean circulation, Dansgaard-Oeschger, ice core
Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

item.title: The rise and fall of a volcanic plateau: Landscape evolution at the fringes of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet, Meseta Chile Chico, central Patagonian Andes
item.dc:creator: Carolina Franco, Emma-Louise Cooper, Antonio Maldonado, María Eugenia de Porras, Amalia Nuevo Delaunay, César Méndez, … (+3)
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: ice sheet, buttressing, glacier, paleoclimate, last glacial maximum, Holocene, Pliocene, climate change
ABSTRACT Understanding Earth‐surface processes along the fringes of large ice sheets is integral to deciphering cold‐region environmental variability and anticipating slope instability under climate change. We investigate the Meseta Chile Chico, a volcanic plateau in the central Patagonian Andes, located at the eastern margin of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet. Here, glacier retreat patterns are well‐constrained, while the influence of periglacial, paraglacial, and postglacial processes is not. We employ geomorphological mapping integrated with geological and palaeoclimate reconstructions to provide a spatio‐temporal model of landscape evolution. Enhanced erosion since the late Pliocene, caused by differential tectonic uplift and glacial isostatic rebound, produced the rugged morphology that characterizes the Meseta Chile Chico. During the Last Glacial Maximum, glaciers occupied surrounding valleys, while the surface of the plateau was reshaped by long‐lasting periglacial freeze‐thaw cycles and nivation. Postglacial landscape adjustment included intensified landslide activity along the edges of the plateau (linked to paraglacial de‐buttressing at its bordering valleys) and regional base‐level changes. During the Holocene, flow‐type landslides became increasingly controlled by climatic variability. The geomorphology of the Meseta Chile Chico reflects an interplay between inherited geology, (de)glaciation, and climate, highlighting the importance of an interdisciplinary approach for understanding recent landscape dynamics in deglaciating mountain regions.

item.title: Assessing the potential of Individual Foraminifera Analyses (δ18O) to reconstruct variability, seasonality and extremes in the tropical Indian Ocean
item.dc:creator: Yohan Lichterfeld, Guillaume Leduc, Kaustubh Thirumalai, Laurence Vidal, Thibault de Garidel-Thoron, Corinne Sonzogni, … (+1)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: oxygen isotope, d18O, foraminifera, extreme event, climate extreme
The Indian Ocean regulates global climate through heat and moisture exchanges. To understand past climate variability, we analyzed oxygen isotopes in individual fossil shells of tiny marine organisms. Combining numerical simulations, we show that shell chemistry reflects seasonal temperature changes driven by both the monsoon and the Indian Ocean Dipole. This opens new perspectives for reconstructing past climate extreme events.

item.title: Holocene Paleoenvironmental Evolution Recorded in Nearshore Deposits from the Zhejiang Coast
item.dc:creator: Shengdong Xu, Yao Zhang, Dingyi Zhao, Junjie Zhang, Pinjing Chen, Zhenhao Zhu, … (+3)
item.description:
Geosciences — matched: deglaciation, Holocene, proxy
The Zhejiang region preserves a complete evolutionary trajectory from hunter-gatherer to early state-level societies, which offers critical material for examining social complexity. Nevertheless, the lack of continuous, high-quality Holocene paleoenvironmental archives in this area hampers a thorough assessment of the human–environment interaction over time. This study investigates pollen, ostracod, foraminiferal and particle-size proxies to reconstruct regional environmental dynamics from core TQ1 in Taizhou Bay spanning 14.8–0.4 cal ka BP based on AMS 14C dating. Core TQ1 records a transition from predominantly terrestrial influence during the late deglaciation to increasing marine influence during the early Holocene. Based on paleoenvironmental changes, the Holocene can be further divided into three stages. Stage 1 (11.5–8.5 cal ka BP) was characterized by a coastal environment with stronger hydrodynamics; arboreal pollen declined while herbs, ferns and algae increased. Stage 2 (8.5–4.2 cal ka BP) represented the peak transgression with open marine conditions and maximum microfossil abundance, and forest recovery as terrestrial herbs and algae decreased. Stage 3 (4.2–0.4 cal ka BP) shifted back to nearshore shallow-sea conditions, with persistently high arboreal percentages and sustained pollen input from forested terrestrial source areas. The intense paleoenvironmental changes, coupled with the evolutionary processes of ancient cultures in the adjacent areas, provide new evidence for a deeper understanding of regional cultural evolution.

item.title: Loss of snow persistence during late season drives snow-season shortening in Northeast China under global warming
item.dc:creator: Yao Xiao, Guojie Hu, Ren Li, Guangyue Liu, Tonghua Wu, Xiaodong Wu, … (+2)
item.description:
Communications Earth & Environment — matched: CMIP, emulator, machine learning, global warming
Northeast China lies on a mid-latitude boundary where small warming can shift snowfall to rain and shorten the snow season, but climate models often simulate snow fields with large regional biases. Here we show that satellite-constrained, 1-km machine-learning emulators project snow-cover duration without directly using modeled snow variables. They relate observed daily snow cover during 2001–2020 to temperature, precipitation, snowfall fraction and terrain, and are driven by bias-corrected climate projections. Snow seasons shorten almost everywhere, with more than 98% of land grid cells agreeing on the sign of change. By 2081–2100, domain-mean snow-cover duration decreases by 42, 64, and 85 days under low-, intermediate- and high-emission pathways, respectively, and areas with fewer than 50 snow days expand from 19% to 99% under high emissions. Snow-season shortening is dominated by loss of late-winter and spring snow persistence, especially at low–middle elevations and along the present rain–snow transition zone. The loss of snow persistence during late winter to spring across Northeast China leads to shorter snow season under global warming, as suggested by bias-corrected CMIP6 climate projections based on Satellite-constrained machine learning framework.

item.title: Forest or tundra? How different vegetation reconstructions of Last Glacial landscapes in Europe may shape our perception of early human dispersal processes
item.dc:creator: Oliver A. Kern, Anne Dallmeyer, Andreas Maier, Philipp Schlüter, Annika Vogel, Nikki Vercauteren
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: boreal forest
ABSTRACT Regional variability and long‐term changes of past ecosystems likely had a strong impact on hunter–gatherer population dynamics, including the expansion of anatomically modern humans and the disappearance of Neanderthals. However, our understanding of these ecosystems remains limited, even when looking at large‐scale patterns, such as the extent and distribution of forested areas. Vegetation reconstructions are key to better understanding ecological preferences and their influence on the spatial distribution and dispersals of early humans. Here, we compare four different vegetation reconstruction techniques, two based on pollen data and two vegetation models, between 70 and 20 thousand years before present in Europe. Absolute values in forest cover can differ by up to 40% between reconstruction techniques, highlighting that the choice of method can make the difference between a boreal forest and a tundra. Besides method‐specific and statistical uncertainties, the reason for such a substantial offset lies in the loose definition of forest cover metrics, rendering a direct comparison between methods impossible. At the same time, we show that all reconstruction techniques accurately reconstruct ecosystem dynamics over time on continental to regional scales. We therefore highly recommend that researchers use relative forest cover measures as the more robust method to estimate past landscapes.

item.title: Glaciotectonic Spectrum
item.dc:creator: James Sandusky Aber, Susan Ward Aber
item.category: Transactions of the Kansas Academy of Science
item.description:
Transactions of the Kansas Academy of Science — matched: ice sheet
Glaciotectonic landforms include a spectrum of hill-hole pairs, composite ridges, push moraines, cupola hills, and drumlins with deformed internal structures. Their regional distribution as well as buried glaciotectonic features are reviewed with an emphasis on Scandinavia, adjacent Russia, and Baltic nations. LiDAR and ground investigations were the keys for recognizing murtoos as a new category of distinct glaciotectonic landforms, which are particularly well documented in Finland and Sweden. Three main zones of glacial landscapes are recognized for ice-sheet glaciation - outer, intermediate, and inner, as well as a transitional boundary between the outer and intermediate zones. Glaciotectonic phenomena are numerous and widespread in all of these zones wherever the substratum consists of sedimentary bedrock or unconsolidated sediments.
